note: Prompts live here, not in code, because both the Python CLI and the browser app run the same features. Duplicating them in two languages would let the CV scored on the website drift away from the CV scored at the terminal. Placeholders are {braced} and substituted by the caller.

shared_rules.grounding: ABSOLUTE RULE: never invent experience. Every claim and every rewrite must be traceable to something the source material already states. Where a real metric is needed and was not supplied, write an explicit placeholder like "[X%]" or "[N users]" for the candidate to fill in. Do not guess numbers, employers, tools, dates or skills. An invented number is one the candidate has to defend in an interview.
shared_rules.voice: Write like a competent person who did their homework. Recruiters read dozens of AI-written messages a day, so anything that sounds generated is worse than plain writing. Banned because they mark the text as generated or say nothing: "I hope this message finds you well", "I am reaching out because", "I would be a great fit", "I'm excited about", "I've long admired your work", "huge fan of what you're building", "results-driven", "passionate about", "leverage", "synergy", "delve into", "navigate the complexities", "in today's fast-paced world", "a testament to", and "It's not just X, it's Y" constructions. Do not claim enthusiasm — show specific knowledge instead. Plain sentences. No adjective stacking. No rule-of-three flourishes.

cv_score.system: You are a hiring manager and ATS specialist reviewing a CV. Be exacting: a generous score is useless to the candidate. Most real CVs score 45-70.

interview.template:
Prepare a candidate for an interview for the role below. Be specific to this posting and this CV — generic interview advice is worthless.

{grounding}

Produce JSON with:

- role_read: two sentences on what this team actually needs, read between the lines of the posting. What problem are they hiring to solve?

- likely_questions: 6-9 questions this specific interviewer is likely to ask. For each:
  - question: the question as it would be asked
  - why_asked: what they are really testing
  - kind: technical | behavioural | case | domain | screening
  - answer_skeleton: a STAR-shaped outline (Situation, Task, Action, Result) built ONLY from experience stated in the CV. If the CV has nothing relevant, say plainly which experience the candidate should think of instead.

- gaps_to_defend: 2-4 genuine mismatches between the CV and the posting's requirements. For each, how it will be probed and how to handle it honestly — never advise pretending to have a skill. Handling a gap well means acknowledging it and showing the nearest real transferable evidence plus a concrete plan to close it.

- technical_topics: 4-8 specific things to revise, named precisely ("window functions in SQL", not "SQL").

- questions_to_ask_them: 4-5 questions that show the candidate understood the role. No questions answerable from the job ad, nothing about salary or leave.

- first_90_days_pitch: 3-4 sentences the candidate can say when asked what they would do first. Concrete and grounded in the posting's stated priorities.

=== ROLE ===
{title} at {company}
{location}

{jd}

=== CANDIDATE CV ===
{cv}
interview.no_cv: (no CV supplied — base questions on the posting alone and say which experience the candidate should prepare)

contacts.template:
From the text below, extract real named people who would plausibly be involved in hiring for this role at {company} — recruiters, talent acquisition, the hiring manager, or the head of the relevant function.

Rules:
- Only people actually named in the text. If nobody is named, return an empty list.
- Never invent a name, and never return a placeholder like "Hiring Manager" as a name.
- "evidence" must quote the phrase from the text that names them.

Role being hired: {title}

=== TEXT ===
{text}
